stimulus.text: Emanuel Bowen's chart of the Atlantic Ocean, published in London on 5 September 1740. It maps the Atlantic between the Americas on the left and Europe and Africa on the right, with rhumb lines radiating from compass roses across the whole ocean. The words 'the Trade Winds' appear twice across the middle of the ocean. Its full title reads: 'A new chart of the vast Atlantic Ocean; exhibiting the seat of war, both in Europe and America, likewise the trade winds and course of sailing from one continent to the other.'

stem: This 1740 English chart of the Atlantic Ocean carefully maps the trade winds and 'the course of sailing from one continent to the other.' What does the chart's focus on winds and sailing courses reveal about transatlantic commerce?

options.text: Steamships had replaced sailing vessels by 1740
options.misconception: Puts steam a century too early; 1740 Atlantic trade ran on wind.

options.text: Merchants depended on predictable wind patterns to move their ships
England had little interest in Atlantic trade at the time
options.misconception: Reads a trade chart as indifference; the chart exists because the trade mattered.

options.text: The chart was designed to discourage merchants from attempting dangerous voyages
options.misconception: Mistakes a navigational tool for a warning; the chart maps courses to follow.

rationales.general:
1. Look at what the chart labels. 'The Trade Winds' appears twice, and the title promises the course of sailing.
2. Ask why a chart-maker would draw that. Winds were the engine of Atlantic travel — ships went where the winds took them.
3. Read the purpose. The chart is a tool for merchants and captains, not a decoration.
4. Rule out the rest. Steam came decades later, and a chart full of trade routes shows interest, not indifference.
Remember: on an old map, what is labeled loudest is what mattered most to its makers.
rationales.A: Steamships did not appear until the 1800s. In 1740 the Atlantic ran on wind and sail.
rationales.B: The chart maps the winds because ships depended on them — the winds set the sailing courses.
rationales.C: A chart packed with trade routes and sailing courses shows deep interest in Atlantic trade, not indifference.
rationales.D: The chart guides merchants across the ocean; it maps the courses, it does not warn them away.
